Sharon Claydon The question is that the amendments moved by the member for Kooyong be agreed to. Anika Wells I thank the member for Kooyong for moving these amendments. The government will not support the amendments. We do not support imposing new reporting obligations through this bill. These amendments would create a new regulatory reporting regime for sporting, cultural and recreational organisations with annual turnover above $50 million requiring disclosure of gambling related revenue and publication by ACMA. This proposal is outside the scope of the bill's aim to directly reduce harm from gambling and would impose additional compliance and administrative burdens without a demonstrated impact. The government agrees that more must be done to stop gambling advertising from proliferating online. The restrictions introduced by the government ban wagering advertising online by default, unless online content services implement the triple lock requirements—that is, users must be over 18 years of age, logged into an account and have not opted out of wagering advertising. The government takes seriously our responsibility to protect Australians, particularly children and young people, from the harms of online gambling. The government has supported an amendment to establish a wagering advertising opt out register to provide individuals with a one stop shop to opt out of receiving all wagering advertising content. We have worked constructively with the opposition and the crossbench to consider practical amendments to this bill, and I'd like to thank my shadow counterpart, Senator Henderson, in the other place for working with me diligently over a number of weeks in order to get this ready for consideration today in the House. I thank you for your conscientious work, Senator Henderson, and I thank the House. Question negatived. Long debate text truncated.

Moved the second reading of the Interactive Gambling Amendment (Gambling Reform) Bill 2026 and two companion cost-recovery bills, agreed with the Coalition and Senator Henderson, that would restrict wagering advertising during children's programming and live sport, require a triple-lock age-verification and opt-out system, create a Wagering Advertising Opt-out Register funded by a levy on wagering providers, ban inducement marketing to vulnerable customers and BetStop deregistrants, and prohibit online keno and foreign-matched lotteries, noting a February 2026 statutory review found only one in four Australians know BetStop exists; a Coalition senator welcomed the amendments strengthening protections while criticising the original bill and the government's handling of the reforms.
This bill strengthens how the social media minimum age framework is enforced.
It expands the eSafety Commissioner's powers to demand documents and information from anyone relevant to compliance checks.
Civil penalties for breaking minimum age rules would double to 60,000 penalty units, worth about $99 million for a body corporate.
Expands the eSafety Commissioner's information-gathering powers to compel production of documents from any person.
Doubles the maximum civil penalty for contraventions of Division 2, Part 4A from 30,000 to 60,000 penalty units.
Increases the maximum civil penalty for contraventions of Division 4, Part 4A from 500 to 1,000 penalty units.
Providers of age-restricted social media platforms and the eSafety Commissioner are affected.

Tony Pasin I feel a little like an imposter talking on this bill. Many of my colleagues who know me know that I'm probably best described as a Luddite. Even as a Luddite, in this role one has to be across the role of online presences. In fact, I am wanted, recently, to describe myself to colleagues, members of the party and constituents otherwise as a 'content creator'. I've got to tell you, Mr Deputy Speaker, when I entered the parliament in 2013, if someone told me it was a condition of this role that I would have to become a digital content creator, I would have stayed in the law and transitioned to the farm. I wouldn't have sought preselection. I wouldn't have worked very hard to obtain that preselection and then worked very hard during the election of 2013 and subsequent elections since then. But the truth is that, in the modern age, if you want to share and communicate with your constituency, or if you're in business and you want to share and communicate with customers, if you're not on a digital platform then you're missing out. And young people have gained aptitude towards digital acumen faster than any other cohort in the country. I've got a 16-year-old and a 10-year-old, and their acumen around digital platforms and these things is just a sight to behold. I'm not one of those people who come in here and say that everything about online experiences is wrong. I don't conform to that view. Like everything, there need to be appropriate safeguards; there need to be appropriate barriers. That is what we're seeking to achieve here, and I of course support my colleague the member for Lindsay's amendment. But it is important that we understand that, as positive as experiences can be in the digital online environment, there are also substantial risks. Like others, I've read of very tragic circumstances. I've had constituents, parents, come to me concerned about the way algorithms are seeking to lock young people in. This bill is part of a package that would change how capital gains are taxed, replacing the current discount system.
The package would introduce a tax floor on gains and update the method for calculating taxable profit to reflect inflation.
The new rules would start on 1 July 2027 and would apply to future gains on assets bought before that date, with exceptions for some housing and small businesses.
Replace the 50% capital gains discount for individuals, trusts and partnerships with an indexation system for the cost base.
Create a 30% minimum tax on capital gains, exempting certain income support recipients.
Apply the new rules to gains from 1 July 2027, including those on assets bought before that date, while keeping the discount for new and affordable housing and existing small business concessions.
Individuals, trusts, partnerships, and some income support recipients who make capital gains.

Australia's small businesses are shutting at a disturbing rate: 40,000 microbusinesses lost in four years as wages that they have to pay go up. Admittedly, the workers are getting less bang for their buck, but tax reforms and calls for a three-day week just mount and small business is doing it so very tough. What I fear is that those opposite don't understand or appreciate the hardships of small business because in many cases they have not run one. They've run picket lines out in front of them and they've run them into the ground, but they haven't actually run a small business to save themselves, and they don't understand and appreciate the complexities facing the operators of those many, many small businesses. I ran one for nearly a decade, with a couple of others, and it's tough. Often you take home less pay yourself than you are in fact paying your employees, your workers. As to workers, yes, we saw the independent commission this week give a wage rise to Australia's lowest paid workers—bearing in mind Australia has one of the highest minimum wages anywhere. But I say to those workers: do not be fooled, because once you take away the power bills, the rent or mortgage costs, the grocery bills and the fuel costs, you're taking home less. Monique Ryan While we're making generational changes to Australia's capital gains tax system, we need to ensure that wholesale reforms don't come at the expense of clear modernisations. The thresholds for small businesses claiming capital gains tax exemptions is such an area of clear modernisation. The existing CGT small-business concession regime, the SBC regime, provides a sliding scale of concessional tax treatment to business owners when they sell their businesses. That regime is preserved by this budget. Under the current Income Tax Act 1997, in order to qualify for the regime, small businesses must have either an aggregated turnover of less than $2 million or combined net assets of less than $6 million. Those thresholds have been unchanged for almost 20 years. The maximum net asset value test was first introduced in 1999, with the Howard government's discount. Moved the Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026, proposing worker tax relief, a $1,000 instant deduction, first-home ownership measures, indexed capital gains taxation and limits on negative gearing for existing residential properties.

Moved that two tax reform bills be referred to the Standing Committee on Economics, arguing that rushed legislation required scrutiny of effects on housing, young people, small businesses, startups, productivity and fairness.

Moved to vary sitting arrangements on 2 and 3 June 2026 to prioritise taxation bills, then moved that debate on two tax reform bills not conclude until every government member had spoken; the motions were agreed to with an absolute majority.
Moved to allow two taxation bills to be debated together and moved that the question be put; the question on the motion was then before the House.

Moved that the Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026 and Income Tax Rates Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026 be referred to the Standing Committee on Economics for an advisory report by 30 December 2026, then moved that government business order No. 2 be called on immediately.

Supported tax reform bills that would replace the capital gains tax concession with cost-base indexation from 1 July 2027, limit negative gearing on later-purchased rental properties to new homes, introduce a $250 working Australian tax offset and create a $1,000 instant deduction, arguing the changes would improve fairness and housing affordability.

Moved to suspend standing and sessional orders so debate on the tax reform bills would not conclude until every government member had spoken, then moved that the question be put and later that debate be adjourned, while arguing members should be accountable for the budget's measures.

Moved that the Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026 and Income Tax Rates Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026 be referred to the Standing Committee on Economics for consideration and an advisory report by 30 December 2026.

Moved to suspend standing and sessional orders so specified amendments and remaining stages of the Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026 and Income Tax Rates Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026 could be grouped, debated briefly, and put to immediate questions, then moved that the question be put.

Argued that the tax reform bills contain welcome measures on property concessions but require fuller scrutiny, and foreshadowed amendments to split the bill, clarify startup and employee equity protections, limit ministerial powers, protect grandfathered concessions, exempt testamentary trusts, add income protections and reinvest revenue in social and affordable housing; other contributions disputed the bills' effects and supported or opposed them.

Moved procedural motions setting the Senate's hours, business sequence and voting limits for 23 to 29 June 2026, including expedited consideration of tax, appropriation, secrecy, workplace-relations and other bills; then argued that the agreed tax reforms would damage home saving, business growth and aspiration, promising their repeal under a future coalition government.

Opposed the Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026 and Income Tax Rates Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026, arguing they would reduce investment, business formation and housing opportunities, and criticised proposed exemptions that would require bureaucrats to determine which businesses are innovative.

Moved opposition amendments to remove the capital gains tax and negative gearing schedules from the Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026, arguing the package would raise taxes, increase compliance costs and harm housing, investment and businesses; the government said those measures funded tax offsets and rebalanced taxation, before the committee reported progress.

Reported and explained government amendments to the tax reform bills, including raising the active-asset concession threshold from $2 million to $10 million, exempting specified income-support recipients from the minimum capital-gains tax, and removing or narrowing ministerial powers; questions and answers addressed projected revenue, compliance costs and classic-car treatment.
Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Act 2026
This bill is part of a package that would change how capital gains are taxed in Australia.
The package would replace the current 50% capital gains tax discount for individuals, trusts and partnerships with a system that adjusts the cost base for inflation, so only real gains are taxed.

It would also introduce a 30% minimum tax on capital gains from 1 July 2027, with an exemption for some income support recipients, while keeping the discount for new and affordable housing and existing small business concessions.
Replace the 50% capital gains tax discount with cost base indexation for individuals, trusts and partnerships.
Introduce a 30% minimum tax on capital gains, exempting certain income support recipients.

Australia’s Foreign Relations (State and Territory Arrangements) Amendment Bill 2026

Speaking for the Coalition, supported the Australia's Foreign Relations (State and Territory Arrangements) Amendment Bill 2026 as a sensible response to the Huxtable review, but argued it leaves a gap allowing direct researcher-to-researcher collaborations with foreign institutions, including reported Iran-linked drone research at Australian universities, to escape Commonwealth notification, and proposed an amendment requiring universities to notify significant staff research collaborations regardless of formal university involvement.
Treasury Laws Amendment (Supporting Choice in Superannuation and Other Measures) Bill 2025

Moved an amendment noting support for Schedules 3, 4 and 6 of the Treasury Laws Amendment (Supporting Choice in Superannuation and Other Measures) Bill 2025, while opposing Schedules 1 and 2 on the grounds that they restrict superannuation choice and competition.

Supported practical housekeeping measures in the Regulatory Reform Omnibus Bill 2025 but argued that it was not substantive reform, and sought removal of the proposed Greenhouse and Energy Minimum Standards Act change while supporting a government amendment addressing fuel security limits.

Supported the appropriation bills to ensure continuity of government services but argued that the government's economic management had weakened living standards, increased spending, debt and taxes, and failed to grow productivity; he called for fiscal rules to contain spending.

Moved and seconded a motion to return the Electricity Infrastructure Legislation Amendment Bill 2025 from the Federation Chamber to the House, arguing that its retrospective changes to offshore wind licensing required parliamentary scrutiny; the question was deferred and debate adjourned.

The coalition opposed the Safeguard Mechanism (Crediting) Amendment Bill 2022, arguing it imposes a hidden carbon tax of $75 per tonne that will raise costs for consumers and force businesses to close, while Labor and Greens speakers supported the bill as necessary to meet Australia's 43% emissions reduction target by 2030 and net zero by 2050.

The government abandoned its election promise to cut household power bills by $275, legislating only a 43% emissions reduction target without any price protections, while the bill's consequential amendments risk enabling green lawfare and restricting agencies like Export Finance Australia, Infrastructure Australia and the Northern Australia Infrastructure Fund.
